messages.subject: Sample size question?
parts:
Hi all,
I am a beginner with SEM and lavaan. So, I am really sorry that my questions may seem dumb.
I am running quite a complex model. It has 485 free parameters and 37 equality constraints. I have a sample of 207 observations (or units). My data is longitudinal with two time points. So, in total, I have 414 data points.
When I ran the model, everything looks fine. It converged to a solution and the global fitness indices seem fine. The only warning I received is:

"In lav_object_post_check(object) :
  lavaan WARNING: some estimated lv variances are negative"

In fact, I have only 2 latent variables in the model and the variance of one of them is negative.

So:
1) Can anyone help me figure out how to deal with the warning above? Is it serious? I mean given that the model converges to a solution and the fitness indices are fine, what the implication of the warning could be? Is it related to the sample size?
2) Will my sample size be an issue for publication, given that the are more parameters than observations (or units) in my model?

Thank you so much,

Ranaivo

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Sample size question?
parts: I have a sample of 207 observations (or units). My data is longitudinal with two time points. So, in total, I have 414 data points.

Not if your data are in wide format.  Then you would still have N=207 but twice as many variables (2 occasions).  If you are storing your occasions in long format, you are violating your independence assumption, unless you use ML-SEM with persons as clusters.

"In lav_object_post_check(object) :
  lavaan WARNING: some estimated lv variances are negative"

In fact, I have only 2 latent variables in the model and the variance of one of them is negative.

So:
1) Can anyone help me figure out how to deal with the warning above? Is it serious?
I don't understand your question.  You yourself verified that the message is correct: you have 2 latent variables, one of their variance estimates was negative.
I mean given that the model converges to a solution and the fitness indices are fine, what the implication of the warning could be? Is it related to the sample size?

Variances can be estimated as negative because of gross model misspecification (apparently not the case here?) or just due to sampling error.  It will happen more often the closer the true parameter is to zero and the smaller the sample is.  You can check whether the interval estimate includes positive values, in which case you can't reject the H0 that the true variance is nonnegative:

summary(fit, ci = TRUE)
2) Will my sample size be an issue for publication, given that the are more parameters than observations (or units) in my model?

Frankly, I think it should be.  To have any confidence in so many simultaneously estimated parameters, you need enough data to support it.  Using insufficient samples is one of the (many) root causes of the replicability crisis.  It is not just that your Type II error rate is high (low power), but when you make Type I errors, the estimated effect size must by definition be quite large to have been (incorrectly) flagged as significant.  Or even if there really is an effect, detecting it as significant will only happen when it is over estimated to a large degree, which makes it harder to trust even meta-analyses that accumulate information filtered by publication bias, etc.

Is it possible to isolate particular hypotheses you want to test, that could be addressed with reduced models of a subset of variables at a time?  Sharing your syntax would help provide more well-informed advice.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

Your idea about splitting the "big" model into smaller models sounds interesting. Perhaps, I can do that and if the patterns in the smaller models are similar to those in the big models, that may mean that the big model is not so bad. Does that sound a reasonable approach?

Any advice you can provide will be appreciated.

Many thanks,

Ranaivo
